title: Bibliometric analysis of radiology residency theses in Türkiye: publication metrics and trends

sections.title: Why Turkish Residency Theses Are Worth Counting
sections.markdown:
In Türkiye, every doctor training in a medical specialty has to write an original thesis before sitting the specialty exam. It is a legal requirement, written into the country's regulation on specialty training, and similar rules exist in parts of Europe. That means decades of research sitting in a national archive. The question this study asks is simple: how much of that work ever reaches a journal, and what separates the theses that get published from the ones that do not?

The method used to answer it is **bibliometrics**, the statistical analysis of academic documents. Bibliometric studies count things like publication rates, citations, and topic distributions to reveal where a field's attention goes and where the gaps are. Other Turkish specialties (anesthesiology, general surgery, neurosurgery, family medicine) have been analyzed this way. Radiology had not been, and this is the first study to cover it.

sections.title: How the Theses Were Collected, Classified, and Tracked
sections.markdown:
## What they did

The team pulled every radiology residency thesis from the online database of the National Thesis Center of Türkiye's Council of Higher Education, searching under both "Radiology" and "Radiodiagnostics" with no date limit. After removing theses with missing data, access restrictions, or wrong department labels, 3,136 theses remained, spanning 1971 through December 2024. Theses dated January 2025 or later were dropped on the reasoning that turning a thesis into a paper takes at least six months, so recent ones would look unpublished simply because there had not been time.

For each thesis they recorded the title, the author's gender, the advisor's gender and academic title, page count, year, institution name and type, number of advisors, study design, and sample size. Where two advisors were listed, the one with the higher academic rank was treated as primary.

Two radiology consultants sorted every thesis into one of 14 subspecialty groups drawn from the Turkish Society of Radiology's scientific research groupings: neuroradiology, head and neck, musculoskeletal, breast, thoracic, abdominal, genitourinary, interventional, cardiovascular, imaging physics and radiation safety, obstetric, emergency, pediatric, and "other." They reached agreement on all of them.

Then came the manual part. To find out whether a thesis had become a paper, the authors searched the thesis author's name, the advisor's name, and relevant keywords across Google, Google Scholar, PubMed, Web of Science, TR Index (Türkiye's national citation index), and DergiPark (a Turkish academic publishing platform). Conference abstracts and presentations were not counted. When a matching article turned up, they logged the journal, country, publication year, whether the resident was first author, citation counts from Google Scholar and PubMed, and how the journal was indexed at the time the article appeared.

Two derived measures carry most of the analysis:

publication rate = (number of theses found as published articles / total theses) x 100

This is the share of theses that made it into a peer-reviewed journal.

time to publication = article publication date - thesis completion date, measured in days

This is how long the thesis-to-paper conversion took.

Journals were sorted into a five-tier hierarchy: Science Citation Index Expanded (**SCIE**, the highest tier), Emerging Sources Citation Index (**ESCI**, a Web of Science category for newer or regionally focused journals), other international journals outside Web of Science, national journals in TR Index, and national journals outside it. A journal listed in more than one database was counted only at its highest tier. For SCIE journals, the authors also recorded the impact factor quartile (Q1 through Q4) from Journal Citation Reports for the year of publication, where Q1 means the top quarter of journals in that field.

Statistics were standard for this kind of data: chi-squared tests for categorical comparisons, Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis for skewed continuous variables like citation counts, Poisson regression for the annual thesis count, and logistic regression for publication probability by year. Significance was set at P below 0.05.

sections.title: Publication Rates, Timing, and What Predicted Success
sections.markdown:
## What they found

The structural picture first. Most theses (83.1%) came out of university hospitals rather than training and research hospitals, and most were supervised by senior faculty: 45.8% by professors, 33.4% by associate professors. Thesis output rose sharply after 2000, peaking at 198 in 2010. The authors tie this to expanding residency quotas, which went from 38 positions in 2008 to 105 in 2018, and note that a sevenfold quota increase after 2022 should show up in thesis counts within a few years, since training lasts five.

Topic choice clustered heavily. Neuroradiology (16.0%), abdominal radiology (13.3%), and interventional radiology (12.4%) were the three most common subjects. Imaging physics and radiation safety came last at 1.6%, with obstetric radiology similarly thin. The authors read the top three as tracking clinical exposure: broad patient populations, varied imaging techniques, and 15 months of combined training time in the official curriculum.

The headline number: **1,165 of 3,136 theses (37.1%) were published** as journal articles. Of all theses, 20.8% (n = 651) landed in SCIE-indexed journals. Looking only at the theses that did get published, 55.9% went to SCIE journals. But quality within that tier skewed low. Of the 651 SCIE articles, 456 (39.2% of published articles) appeared in Q3 or Q4 journals, the bottom half of the impact factor distribution. Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology (7.0%) and the European Journal of Radiology (4.2%) were the most common destinations.

Timing was slow. The gap between thesis completion and publication ranged from 151 days to 11,680 days, with a median of 1,300 days (roughly three and a half years) and a mean of about 1,663 days. Citations were modest: median 3 per article, mean 14.7, range 0 to 416. The resident was first author on 76.4% of published articles, the advisor on 12.9%, and someone else on 10.7%.

Two trends moved in the right direction over time. The probability that a thesis got published rose significantly (P = 0.045), and time to publication fell significantly (P < 0.001). Both shifts concentrated after 2000. For scale, an earlier study by Ozgen and colleagues covering 1980 to 2005 found that only 6.3% of radiology theses reached SCIE journals; this study's 20.8% across 1971 to 2024 represents a large improvement.

Several comparisons that might have been expected to matter did not. Thesis topic showed no significant relationship with publication rate, citations, or time to publication. Publication rates by subspecialty ranged from 51.0% for imaging physics and radiation safety down to 32.6% for breast radiology, but the spread was not statistically significant. Advisor gender made no difference to anything measured. Resident gender made no difference to publication rate or citations, though theses by female residents took significantly longer to reach publication (P < 0.001), matching findings from psychiatry and ophthalmology.

Three findings did hold up:

- **Advisor rank cut against seniority.** Theses supervised by assistant professors had the highest publication rate at 43.0%, significantly above professors (34.8%) and associate professors. The authors attribute this to faculty who are mid-promotion having a stronger personal stake in getting papers out. The same pattern appears in anesthesiology, otorhinolaryngology, and plastic surgery.
- **Institution type affected citations, not output.** University hospitals and training and research hospitals published at similar rates and similar speeds, but university publications drew significantly more citations (P < 0.001).
- **First authorship predicted everything.** When the advisor or another researcher led the paper, it reached an SCIE journal 74.7% or 69.6% of the time, versus 50.8% when the resident led. Those articles also collected more citations and appeared faster (all P < 0.001). The likely explanation is experience: knowing how to write for journals, how to pick a target, and how to manage revisions.

sections.title: The Quality Ceiling and What Should Change
sections.markdown:
## Why it matters

Placed against other Turkish specialties, radiology sits in the upper-middle range. Its publication rate beats anesthesiology, general surgery, public health, family medicine, physical medicine and rehabilitation, and emergency medicine, and trails thoracic surgery, child and adolescent psychiatry, and endocrinology. Cross-specialty comparisons are noisy, since studies differ in period covered, indexing rules, and methods.

The quality ceiling is the more interesting problem. Getting into SCIE at all is one bar; getting into Q1 or Q2 is another, and most of these papers cleared only the first. The authors point to study design as one likely cause, since 86.7% of the theses were retrospective, and prospective and experimental work tends to publish more often and in stronger journals. They also raise a structural reason that has nothing to do with science: article processing charges. Turkish researchers value journal prestige, but high open-access fees push some toward cheaper, lower-impact venues.

The underrepresentation of imaging physics and radiation safety draws a pointed comment. Radiology personnel in Türkiye have documented gaps in radiation safety knowledge, and physics governs image quality, yet the topic drew 1.6% of theses. Obstetric radiology's low share is linked to short training time, thin theoretical content, and the fact that obstetricians perform most obstetric imaging in Türkiye, so residents get little exposure.

The recommendations follow from the data: strengthen mentorship, give residents structured training in academic writing and journal selection (the three-and-a-half-year median lag suggests they are working without much support), invest in institutional research infrastructure so publications get read as well as printed, and encourage stronger study designs. The framing the authors push is that a residency thesis is a piece of scholarly work with a publication plan attached, and it should be treated that way from the start.

sections.title: What the Study Could Not Capture
sections.markdown:
## Limitations

Publication status was checked only through online databases, so articles in local or low-visibility journals may have been missed. Scopus was not queried separately, and anything indexed exclusively there could have been overlooked. Thesis-to-article matching relied on name and content similarity rather than direct verification, which allows occasional mismatches. Conference abstracts, proceedings, and book chapters were excluded. Citation counts are a snapshot and understate long-term impact for recent papers. And because conversion typically takes more than two years, theses from 2023 and 2024 are likely undercounted, which biases the recent publication rate downward.
